lead: A blockchain has no manager. Many equal computers must still agree on one order of blocks, even when some are slow, disconnected or dishonest. The rules that produce that agreement are the consensus mechanism. Consensus stops the same coin being spent twice, because every honest node decides which transaction came first. This chapter defines consensus, lists the properties it must have, counts how many faulty nodes a network can survive, and sorts the named mechanisms into families: proof-based, voting-based, round robin and hybrids.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for public, private and consortium chains, and 3.1 for how equal nodes reach each other without a server.

blocks.text: A consensus mechanism (some syllabi say consensus algorithm or consensus protocol) is the set of rules by which independent nodes agree on one ordered history of blocks. Each node keeps its own copy of the chain, and the mechanism makes every honest copy identical, link by link.
Three properties are checked in every correctness proof.

items: Agreement: no two honest nodes decide different blocks at the same height.
Validity: the decided block was really proposed and its transactions are valid; the protocol cannot invent a block.
Termination: every honest node eventually decides. Blockchain versions often weaken this to 'eventually, with very high probability'.

blocks.text: Two kinds of failure make this hard. A crash fault is a node that simply stops; silence is easy to catch with a timeout. A Byzantine fault is a node that keeps talking but lies, showing different blocks to different peers. A Byzantine node may also stay silent, so Byzantine fault tolerance covers crash faults but not the reverse.

Two obstacles sit on top: network delay, so messages arrive late and out of order, and message loss. The same problem appears outside blockchains, where Raft and Paxos order writes in a database cluster.

sections.h3: How many faulty nodes a network can survive

blocks.text: Let n be the number of nodes and f the number of faulty nodes the network must tolerate. Two bounds are standard.
crash faults: n ≥ 2f + 1;  Byzantine faults: n ≥ 3f + 1;  quorum = 2f + 1
blocks.where: n is the total number of nodes; f is the number of faulty nodes to be tolerated; quorum is the number of matching votes needed to decide a block in a Byzantine fault tolerant protocol. The first bound assumes nodes only stop; the second assumes some nodes may lie.

blocks.text: Why n ≥ 2f + 1 for crashes: with a majority quorum of f + 1 votes, any two quorums share at least one node, and a node that missed a round learns the latest decision from that shared node. With n = 5 and f = 2, the quorum is 3.

Why n ≥ 3f + 1 for Byzantine faults: the f liars can vote with either side of a split. With a quorum of 2f + 1, any two quorums overlap in at least f + 1 nodes. At most f of those are liars, so at least one honest node sees both sides and refuses to back two conflicting blocks.

Proof-based mechanisms give the right to propose a block to whoever shows a scarce resource. Proof of Work uses hashing power, Proof of Stake uses locked coins, Proof of Elapsed Time uses a random wait enforced inside a trusted chip, and Proof of Authority uses the reputation of a short approved validator list.

Voting-based mechanisms ask known members to vote. PBFT needs a 2f + 1 quorum and tolerates liars. Raft and Paxos tolerate only crashes. Tendermint is Byzantine fault tolerant and decides once and for all. The Stellar consensus protocol uses quorum slices: each node names a small set of peers it trusts, and the slices must overlap.

Round robin gives each node a fixed turn: the leader rotates slot by slot, so ordering is cheap, but a silent leader stalls the round until a timeout. Many real systems are hybrids, mixing a proof to pick the proposer with a vote to confirm.

Permissionless networks cannot vote, because one person can create thousands of identities at no cost, a Sybil attack, and free identities would make voting free to capture. A scarce resource makes each identity costly, which is what Sybil resistance means. Permissioned networks already know their members (Unit 1), so voting there is safe, fast and cheap.

Finality differs by family. In probabilistic finality a block can still be replaced, and confidence grows as blocks pile on top. In deterministic finality the block is decided once and cannot be reverted without breaking the protocol rules.

A Proof of Work chain is safe only while no single party controls most of the hashing power. An attacker with more than half the total hash rate can mine a private chain faster than the honest network on average, publish it later, and replace recent blocks. That enables double spending: pay a merchant, let the payment confirm, then release a longer chain in which the payment never happened. It does not let the attacker steal coins, because spending needs private keys, and it cannot cheaply rewrite very old blocks. The defence is economic: honest miners have more to lose.

examples.question: A consortium blockchain runs a Byzantine fault tolerant voting consensus among n = 7 validators. (a) What is the largest number of faulty nodes f it can tolerate? (b) How many votes form the quorum? (c) To tolerate f = 3, what is the minimum n? (d) On a public Proof of Work chain with total hash rate 100 GH/s, an attacker controls 40 GH/s. What share does it hold, and can it outrun the honest chain?
steps: With n = 7: 7 ≥ 3f + 1, so 3f ≤ 6 and f ≤ 2. Largest tolerated f = 2.
40% < 51%, so it cannot outrun the honest chain for long.
examples.answer: f = 2, quorum 5 of 7 votes, minimum n = 10 for f = 3, and the attacker holds 40%, below 51%, so it cannot outrun the honest chain.
examples.check:
n = 7
f = (n - 1) // 3
print(f)
quorum = 2 * f + 1
print(quorum)
f_target = 3
n_min = 3 * f_target + 1
print(n_min)
total = 100
attacker = 40
share = round(attacker / total * 100)
print(share)

traps: Consensus is not the same as mining. Mining is only how Proof of Work reaches consensus; voting-based chains do not mine at all.
Proof of Stake still needs Sybil resistance: the locked stake is the cost that makes fake identities expensive.
Using n ≥ 2f + 1 for Byzantine faults, or a quorum of f + 1. Liars need n ≥ 3f + 1 and a quorum of 2f + 1.
Treating a Proof of Work block as final. It has probabilistic finality only; it becomes very costly, not impossible, to reverse.
Permissioned chains vote because membership is known, not because the members trust each other.

quiz.q: Define a consensus mechanism and name the three properties it must satisfy.
quiz.a: A consensus mechanism is the rule set by which independent nodes agree on one ordered history of blocks. The properties are agreement (no two honest nodes decide different blocks at the same height), validity (the decided block was truly proposed and is valid) and termination (every honest node eventually decides).

quiz.q: State the minimum number of nodes needed to tolerate f Byzantine faults, and the quorum size.
quiz.a: n ≥ 3f + 1 nodes, with a quorum of 2f + 1 matching votes. For crash faults only, n ≥ 2f + 1 is enough.

quiz.q: Why can a permissionless chain not simply vote, while a permissioned chain can?
quiz.a: In an open network one person can create thousands of free identities (a Sybil attack), so votes can be bought without limit. A costly resource such as hashing power or locked coins makes each identity expensive. In a permissioned chain membership is known, so one node is one vote and voting is safe and fast.

quiz.q: Distinguish probabilistic finality from deterministic finality, with one mechanism each.
quiz.a: Probabilistic finality: a block may still be replaced, and the chance falls as more blocks are added on top; Proof of Work works this way. Deterministic finality: the block is decided once and cannot be reverted without breaking the rules; PBFT and Tendermint work this way.

quiz.q: A voting-based chain has n = 13 validator nodes and must tolerate Byzantine faults. Find the largest f and the quorum.
quiz.a: n ≥ 3f + 1 gives 13 ≥ 3f + 1, so 3f ≤ 12 and f ≤ 4, so f = 4. Quorum = 2f + 1 = 2 × 4 + 1 = 9 votes out of 13.

quiz.q: A Proof of Work chain has a total hash rate of 200 GH/s. An attacker controls 90 GH/s. What share does it hold and can it outrun the honest chain?
quiz.a: Share = 90 ÷ 200 × 100 = 45%. The attack needs more than 50%, and 45% < 51%, so the attacker cannot outrun the honest chain for long.

quiz.q: Explain why Byzantine faults need n ≥ 3f + 1 and a quorum of 2f + 1, while crash faults need only n ≥ 2f + 1.
quiz.a: A silent crashing node cannot vote wrongly, so a majority quorum of f + 1 is enough: two quorums always share one node, which carries the latest decision. A lying node can vote on both sides of a split, so the f liars effectively count twice. With n = 3f + 1 and a quorum of 2f + 1 votes, two quorums overlap in at least f + 1 nodes; at most f of those are liars, so at least one honest node sees both proposals and blocks the second. That is why n ≥ 3f + 1 nodes are needed and 2f + 1 votes are needed, that is, why fewer than one third of the network may be faulty.

beyond: Not for the exam. Federated schemes such as the Stellar consensus protocol, and leaderless designs such as Avalanche, replace a single global quorum with overlapping trust sets or repeated random sampling. Modern Byzantine fault tolerant protocols (HotStuff and its descendants) cut the message count so voting consensus runs on hundreds of validators. Search next for quorum intersection, view change and accountable safety, the ideas that make deterministic finality provable.
